backupData.title: This map was built from backup data.
backupData.body: Neither MapNG's own copy of OpenStreetMap nor the live servers could be read, so the roads and buildings came from Overture Maps. It has no lane counts (wide roads can come out as two lanes) and marks bridges only roughly (some come out short or missing). Generate again later for the full detail.

upload.noDataHelpWhat: Some elevation files mark the area outside their survey with a filler number instead of leaving it blank, and don't label it as such. Read literally it becomes flat terrain at that height, walled off from the real ground around it.
upload.noDataHelpFound: This upload has no labelled no-data value, but {value} fills {percent}% of it and sits well outside the real elevation range — so MapNG is treating it as empty. Where your tiles overlap it can then take the real ground from another tile instead of a hole.
upload.noDataHelpOverride: Leave this on Auto unless your data really does have terrain at {value} — a coastline at exactly 0 m, for instance. Then pick None.
upload.layersHelp: Your upload holds more than one survey. The top one is used wherever it has data; each one below fills what the ones above it left empty. Reorder them to change which survey wins where they overlap — newest first by default.

upload.gapFillGpxzHint: Anything your layers don't cover comes from GPXZ, height-matched to your data at the seam.

upload.gapFillNoneHint: Uncovered areas are interpolated from the edges of your data, not from a real dataset.

upload.placedAtCenter: No location in this file: it will be placed at its real size ({w} × {h} m) with its middle on the map's centre. Move the map to where it belongs.
upload.pointSpacing: Point spacing about {cm} cm ({density} points per m²)

upload.resolutionNativeHeavy: At {m} m per pixel the level is {px} × {px} px ({size} m): BeamNG's largest terrain size. Expect long loading, a lot of memory and a slow game on most PCs.

ui.viewDistanceHint: How far the game draws the level. Auto follows the map's size (4 to 16 km). A shorter distance is lighter on a weaker PC.
ui.assumeParkingHint: On: town streets with no parking tags get a parking lane each side (about 2.3 m), as many real streets have. Off: only mapped parking, so those streets come out narrower.
ui.followSurvey: Every road follows the lidar survey
ui.followSurveyHint: On: on lidar (a few metres or finer) every road, primary and secondary roads too, runs at the slope the survey measured along it, 35% at most. Off: tertiary roads and smaller do; main roads keep their class's grade. Motorways and trunk roads always keep their class's grade. Never beside a bridge or tunnel, and not on the global 30 m.
ui.decalSidewalksHint: On: sidewalks and footpaths are flat strips painted on the ground, with no curbs. Quicker to export, a smaller level, and you can drive over them. Off: raised slabs with curbs.
ui.roadSurfaceHint: Decal roads: MapNG's normal roads, painted on the terrain. Mesh Roads (experimental): each paved road also gets a BeamNG Mesh Road under it, saved in the level, for a smooth ride. Hero Roads (experimental): the first time the level loads it builds BeamNG's Hero Road meshes over the roads and bakes them, which takes a minute or two; later loads use the baked meshes. Junctions are not joined yet.
ui.halfAssetsHint: Files for your own tools. Each one downloads on its own.
ui.perTileHint: Off: one file for the whole map. On: the heightmap, the pictures, the road mask, the GeoTIFF and the .ter are made once for each tile, named _tile1, _tile2 and so on.

ui.modelAreaPicking: drag a square on the 2D preview…
ui.meshInfoTiles: Terrain: {k} × {k} tiles of {side} × {side} points, about {size} in all, in one zip. The tiles share their edges.
ui.daeNoTiles: Collada exports one file: choose One file, a wider spacing or a smaller area.
ui.measuredWidths: Road widths from the satellite picture
ui.measuredWidthsOff: Off: roads with no width in OpenStreetMap get their class's usual width. It is set before Generate.
ui.measuredWidthsOnNone: On, but none of this map's roads was measured. Generate again if you turned it on after this map was made.
ui.measuredWidthsUsed: {n} of this map's road pieces use a width measured from the satellite picture.
ui.measuredWidthsUsedOf: {n} of this map's {total} road pieces use a width measured from the satellite picture. The others have a width in OpenStreetMap, or could not be seen clearly enough and keep their class's usual width.
ui.measuredWidthsNowOff: It is switched off now: Generate again to build this map without the measured widths.
ui.curbHeightHint: How far the raised sidewalks stand over the road. Standard is a real curb; Low and Flush are kinder to low cars and easy to drive onto.
ui.viewDistanceShort: How far the game draws the level.
ui.bundleOsm: Include the map data for bug reports
ui.bundleOsmHint: On: the OpenStreetMap data the level was built from goes into the level (levels/<name>/mapng_source/, a few MB at most, which the game never reads), so a report about the level can be rebuilt on exactly the same data. Off: left out.
ui.groundModelsHint: On: the ground is built as 3D models instead of BeamNG's terrain, so a level of several tiles or along a road can be any shape (a long strip of tiles). The level loads slower (its collision is built at load) and has no grass cover; the terrain editor does not work on it. Off: the usual terrain.

weight.summary_extreme: Untested. MapNG was not built for an export of this size. Proceed with caution.
weight.extremeSize: {km} km across with {count} buildings in the area: far past anything MapNG has been tried on. The export may run for hours, stop partway, or make a level the game can't load.
weight.size: {km} km across, corners {far} km from the centre, about {buildings} buildings.
weight.summary_light: Should load and run well on most PCs.
weight.summary_heavy: Needs a capable PC: expect longer loading and lower frame rates in busy areas.
weight.summary_veryHeavy: Many PCs won't load or run it smoothly. You can still export it.
weight.memory_fits: Exporting needs about {gb} GB of memory at its peak; this computer has {total} GB.
weight.memory_tight: Exporting needs about {gb} GB of memory at its peak, close to this computer's {total} GB: close other programs first.
weight.memory_tooMuch: Exporting needs about {gb} GB of memory at its peak, more than this computer's {total} GB can give: it will likely run out. Try a smaller map, or turn buildings off.
weight.webHeavy: This map has {roads} roads. A browser tab can run out of memory building one this dense: the desktop app has no such limit.
weight.farEdge: Its corners are {km} km from the centre. Past about {limit} km BeamNG runs out of precision and objects start to jitter: pick a smaller area or a lower m/px.
weight.nearEdge: Its corners are {km} km from the centre, close to the {limit} km where BeamNG runs out of precision and objects start to jitter.
weight.bigTerrain: A {px} px terrain uses a lot of memory and takes longer to load.
weight.hugeTerrain: A {px} px terrain is beyond what most PCs can hold in memory.
weight.manyBuildings: Build everything is on: all {count} buildings are built. Building meshes are what uses BeamNG's memory: turn Build everything off, or pick a smaller area.
weight.buildingsCapped: {count} buildings in the area: {built} of them are built (Build everything is off).
weight.uncapped: Build everything is on: trees, fences, lamps and props aren't capped either. Dense foliage is what lowers the frame rate most.
weight.squareCrop: This terrain is {w} × {h} px. A BeamNG level is a square with a power-of-two side, so the level will be the middle {size} × {size} px: {pct}% of the area.
weight.squareCropTip: To keep all of it, generate again at {mpp} m/px ({size} px).

A curve never moves more than a little inside the mapped corner (about 3 m for roads, 1 m for railways, 0.75 m for paths), and junctions, track switches and crossings stay exactly where they are mapped. On: every line follows OpenStreetMap point to point, for maps whose data you have already fixed by hand.

disclaimer.lead: Please be aware that all terrain data, heightmaps and 3D models generated by MapNG are estimations based on available elevation, satellite and OpenStreetMap data, so they are only as good as those sources.
disclaimer.resolutionBody: Heightmaps are exported using the selected processing resolution to keep scaling consistent in game engines. When using the global 30 m dataset, terrain is still upsampled, so it remains smoother and less detailed than native high-resolution sources like USGS or GPXZ.
disclaimer.computerBody: Building a map is heavy work. A large or detailed map can use all of your computer's memory or fill its disk, and the browser, MapNG, the game or the whole computer can slow down, freeze or crash, with unsaved work in other programs lost. MapNG warns about very heavy maps, but it cannot know what your computer can take.
disclaimer.noWarranty: MapNG is free software, provided as it is and with no warranty of any kind. You use it at your own risk: its developer is not responsible for any damage to, or loss on, your computer, your files, your game or anything else.
disclaimer.usage: This tool is intended for modding and creative use. It should not be used for navigation, engineering, or critical real-world planning.

about.title: About MapNG
about.subtitle: Real-world maps for BeamNG.drive
about.hero: MapNG turns any real-world location into a playable BeamNG.drive level: terrain, textures, roads with markings and traffic signals, buildings, bridges, vegetation and more, built in your browser or in the free desktop app for Windows and Linux.
about.whatBody: Pick a location, choose an elevation source and generate. The 2D preview shows what will be built, with relief, slope and height views; the 3D preview lets you look round. Then export a complete BeamNG level ZIP built from real elevation and OpenStreetMap data, or take GeoTIFF and GeoJSON data into your own workflow. Add tiles to build one level of any shape, or pick a road and build the level along it.
elevationItems: Global 30 m (AWS Terrain Tiles, mostly SRTM): the fallback where there's no lidar, or on its own; roads smoothed and levelled and rivers kept below their banks automatically; buildings, trees and viaduct decks taken out automatically
Mapterhorn, the default: Mapterhorn's free lidar where a national survey exists (much of Europe, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, parts of the US and Canada), the global 30 m elsewhere; no key needed
USGS 1 m DEM (USA: CONUS, Alaska, Hawaii)
GPXZ (global high resolution, with your own API key; faster on paid plans)
Your own uploads: LAZ/LAS point clouds, GeoTIFF, ASC, GML/XML (also zipped), layered and reprojected, with gaps filled from the global 30 m or GPXZ and blended seams
previewItems: 2D preview: what will be built, by group, with relief, slope and height views and contour lines
Satellite, OSM, hybrid, Game Texture or plain terrain
3D buildings, trees, bushes and barriers from OSM
Mesh quality from balanced up to full native detail
exportItems: BeamNG level package (.zip), up to 16384 x 16384
GeoTIFF elevation (WGS84 or the source CRS)
Advanced mode adds: 16-bit heightmaps, satellite, OSM, hybrid and Game Texture images, road masks, GLB, DAE and .ter
osmItems: MapNG's own OSM copy, growing region by region toward the whole planet: fast, and unaffected by Overpass outages
Show MapNG OSM coverage outlines those regions on the map
Everywhere else: health-ranked Overpass mirrors with an edge cache
Bring your own Overpass server (Tracestrack, Overspan); MapNG's copy still answers first where it can
A banner tells you when the public Overpass servers are down
Overture Maps adds building heights and the footprints OSM is missing (on by default, under Include OSM features)
If every Overpass server fails, OSM data comes from Overture Maps' monthly release instead, so exports still work
about.resolutionStrong: Output sizes from 512 to 16384 px at any processing scale (m/px).
about.resolutionBody: At 1 m/px that covers 0.26 km² up to 268 km². Global 30 m elevation is upsampled and its roads are smoothed automatically; USGS, GPXZ, NMT and uploads keep their real detail.
about.shapesIntro: Step 1 decides what the map covers. One tile is the usual square; more tiles, or a road, make one level of another shape:
shapesItems: Add tiles beside the first, keep them together on a grid or move them freely, and drag each one on the map
Pick the anchor with one click: any tile, or the centre of them all
Road mode: click a road, set the stretch with a handle at each end and a width either side
One level, with roads, buildings and ground running straight through
Long and diagonal shapes are built in pieces and joined into one level
Share codes, saved settings and the desktop app's Modify carry the tiles or the road
about.beamngBody: A ready-to-drive level ZIP for BeamNG.drive 0.40, built from the real place:
beamngItems: Terrain painted with materials from OSM land use, and from ESA WorldCover land cover where OSM maps none, with a 2x satellite or Game base texture (its water straight from the satellite image, its snow where the land cover has it) you can touch up before export
A regional look chosen from the location and from what covers the land: grass, ground cover, rocks and water
Regional trees from BeamNG's own models, picked from OSM tags and the local climate, planted only where WorldCover sees tree cover (trees OSM maps one by one always stand)
Textured buildings with BeamNG's facades and roofs
DecalRoads with real surfaces, lane markings by country, crosswalks, stop bars, parking lanes and shoulders
Raised sidewalks with curb returns and ramps, and median islands on divided roads
Traffic signals for every approach, road signs, and street lamps that light up at night
Hydrants, bins, benches, utility poles and power lines
Bridges with solved decks, piers and graded abutments; tunnels with portals and lights; concrete arch dams with the road and guardrails along the crest
AI traffic on the road network, road names on the minimap, and fuel stations
A surrounding backdrop and a detailed export_report.txt for troubleshooting
A "How heavy is this level?" check before you export, with BeamNG's size and precision limits (it only warns)
additionalItems: Share your whole setup: a short code or link (works for 24 hours), a long code that never expires, or a file. Paste one on the map to load it; your own keys and servers never go with it
Location search (Nominatim), preset scenic locations and Use my location

Keyless Esri satellite and topo layers (place and road names on satellite), one world with a border at the date line, a scale bar, cursor and crosshair coordinates, a right-click menu, and Ctrl+scroll to zoom on the crosshair
Stage-by-stage progress cards for generation and export, with finished steps and timings
Generation caching and cancel for long-running tasks
Light and dark mode, in 7 languages
Export hotspots: an opt-in glow map of where people export levels
Expand all / Collapse all for the settings sections

privacy.title: How export sharing works
privacy.intro: Sharing is off unless you turn it on. When it's on, MapNG counts where levels are exported, so everyone can see the busy areas on the hotspot map.
privacy.sent: For each level you export: which ~5 km square of the map it's in, and whether it came from the website or the desktop app. The square is worked out on your own computer, so your exact location never leaves it.
privacy.notSent: No name, account, email or device ID. No level name, settings or map data. No exact coordinates. Your IP address is not stored.
privacy.where: In MapNG's own Cloudflare account, in a small database (a Cloudflare Durable Object) that only the MapNG developer can access. Like every request to mapng.com, reports pass through Cloudflare's network.
privacy.how: One row per ~5 km square: how many exports came from the website, how many from the desktop app, and the date of the latest one. Nothing links a row to the people who exported there. To stop spam, the server briefly keeps a scrambled (hashed) form of your IP address in memory to allow at most 30 reports an hour; it is never written to storage and is gone within the hour.
privacy.use: For the hotspot map: the counts per square are what the overlay draws, and anyone can turn it on. And for MapNG's public stats page (mapng.com/stats.html), which adds the same squares up by country. The MapNG developer looks at the same totals to see where MapNG is used, for example to choose which regions get MapNG's own faster OSM data next.
privacy.never: Your data is never sold, never passed to anyone, and never used for advertising or tracking. It appears only as totals: per square on the hotspot map, and per country on the public stats page.
privacy.control: Turn sharing on or off at any time with "Share my exports" in the Map layers box on the map. Turning it off stops reports straight away. Counts already added can't be traced back to you, so they can't be picked out and removed individually.
privacy.readMore: Read the full details: exact data, pipeline and code

spawnPoints.placeHint: Click the map to drop a point; drag before letting go to aim it. Drag a pin to move it, or the white handle at its arrow to turn it.
spawnPoints.empty: Automatic: the car starts on a road near the middle of the map.
spawnPoints.name: Name
spawnPoints.heading: Heading (0° = north)
spawnPoints.noDefault: No point is the spawn (★): the car starts on a road near the middle, as without points.
spawnPoints.snapNote: Each point moves onto the nearest drivable road when exported (bridges and tunnels too) and faces along it; away from roads it stays where placed and faces its arrow.
spawnPoints.introShort: Pick where the car starts and add places to jump to.

backgroundAreas.title: Area Mask
backgroundAreas.intro: Shade the hills you won't drive. They keep their shape but get no buildings, trees, grass or props, and download at lower detail. Draw lines (the map's edge counts as part of an outline), then shade the closed areas, or keep the roads you'll drive.
backgroundAreas.roadsLoading: Finding the roads in this area…
backgroundAreas.roadsFailed: Couldn't load the roads. Try again, or draw lines instead.
backgroundAreas.roadsNone: No drivable roads mapped in this area.
backgroundAreas.locked: The area box is locked while mask areas exist. Remove all of them to move or resize it.
backgroundAreas.lockBody: Mask areas use the box's edges as part of their outlines, and the data is fetched for this exact square. While any exist:
backgroundAreas.lockPoint1: the box can't be moved or resized, and its size and m/px are fixed;
backgroundAreas.lockPoint2: you can still pan and zoom the map to draw;
backgroundAreas.lockPoint3: removing all of them unlocks it.
backgroundAreas.hintLine: Draw from edge to edge, or a closed loop. Hold Space to pan.
backgroundAreas.hintBucket: Click a closed area to make it background.
backgroundAreas.hintErase: Click a line or an Unmask stroke to delete it.
backgroundAreas.hintRoad: Click the roads you'll drive. Everything farther than the width from them becomes background.
backgroundAreas.hintOpen: This line doesn't close an area: end it on the box's edge or another line.
backgroundAreas.hintClosed: Closed. Use Shade area to make an area background.
backgroundAreas.hintShade: Click to make this area background.
backgroundAreas.hintUnshade: Click to make this area drivable again.
backgroundAreas.hintNoAreas: No closed areas yet: draw a line first.
backgroundAreas.hintWhole: That area is the whole map: draw a line that closes it first.
backgroundAreas.hintRoadOn: Keeping {name}: {width} m on each side stays drivable.
backgroundAreas.staleCleared: The mask areas were drawn for a box that has since moved, so they were removed.
backgroundAreas.unmaskShift: Hold Shift to paint background instead. [ ] size the brush, 1 2 3 pick the shape, Space pans.
backgroundAreas.hintUnmask: Paint over background to make it drivable again: brush by hand, drag a box, or draw a lasso around it.
backgroundAreas.hintLassoDrag: Hold the mouse and draw around the area.
backgroundAreas.hintRaw: Paint where roads should stay exactly as the elevation data has them, with no smoothing or levelling. Brush by hand, drag a box, or draw a lasso.
backgroundAreas.rawShift: Hold Shift to smooth again instead. [ ] size the brush, 1 2 3 pick the shape, Space pans.
backgroundAreas.hintRawOn: Roads here keep the terrain as downloaded.
backgroundAreas.statRaw: No smoothing on {pct}% of the square
backgroundAreas.lockedPinned: The area box is locked here so you can zoom and pan to draw (hold Space and drag to move the map with a tool picked).
backgroundAreas.hintTooSmall: This line does close an area, but one too small to shade on a map this size. Draw round a bigger area (about {metres} m across or more).
backgroundAreas.introShort: Shade the hills you won't drive: they keep their shape but get nothing built on them.

build.title: What to build
build.presetHint_all: Everything the map has: roads, structures, buildings, street furniture, trees and water.
build.presetHint_clean: Everything except the clutter you hit while driving: benches, bins, hydrants, poles, gates, speed bumps and parked cars.
build.presetHint_roads: Roads with their markings, signs, lamps, bridges, tunnels and railways, on bare terrain.
build.presetHint_scenery: Terrain with trees, grass, rocks and water: no roads or buildings.
build.presetHint_custom: Your own choice of features below.
build.colourMapIn3d: What will be built is drawn on the 2D preview.
build.followSurvey: main roads keep their class grade

trees.title: Trees picked for this area
trees.fromClimate: No tree records around here: picked from the climate.
trees.note: For woods and trees the map doesn't name. A tree with a species in the map keeps it.
trees.switchHint: For each kind: keep it, leave it out (its trees are planted as the other kinds) or plant another kind in its place. Click a model to leave just that one out.
trees.modelOn: Planted: click to leave this model out
trees.modelOff: Left out: click to plant it again
trees.resetHint: Put every kind back to Keep and every model back on

tune.parkingShort: A parking lane each side of town streets that have no parking tags.
tune.followShort: Roads run at the slope the lidar survey measured.
tune.surface_decal: MapNG's normal roads, painted on the terrain.
tune.surface_mesh: Experimental: each paved road also gets a BeamNG Mesh Road under it, for a smoother ride.
tune.surface_hero: Experimental: BeamNG's Hero Roads are built the first time the level loads (a minute or two). Junctions are not joined yet.
tune.walksShort: Flat painted sidewalks with no curbs, instead of raised slabs.
tune.curbShort: How far raised sidewalks stand over the road.
tune.capsShort: Lifts the limits on buildings, fences, lamps and trees.
tune.widthsOffShort: Off: each road gets its class's usual width.
tune.bundleOsmShort: The map data goes into the level, so reports can be reproduced.
tune.groundModelsShort: The ground as 3D models, any shape; slower to load, no grass cover.

build.bundleOsm: no map data for bug reports

tiles.title: Tiles
tiles.oneHint: One tile makes the usual square map. Add tiles to cover a longer or odd-shaped area as one map.
tiles.togetherHint: Tiles sit side by side on a grid; drag a tile's handle on the map to move it to another spot.
tiles.freeHint: Drag a tile's handle on the map to put it anywhere. Overlaps are fetched once.
tiles.terrain: A square with a power-of-two side: built on BeamNG terrain, as usual.
tiles.models: Not a power-of-two square: the ground is built as 3D models (experimental). It loads slower and has no grass cover.
tiles.islands: Some tiles don't touch the others: they become islands in the level.
tiles.webCap: Too big for the website: this shape covers {km2} km², and the website builds at most {maxKm2} km² (16384² pixels) in any shape. Shorten the stretch, narrow it, use fewer tiles, choose a coarser resolution, or use the desktop app.
tiles.desktopWarn: Past {max} px across: the level may be too big for the game to load.
tiles.chunked: Built in pieces (experimental): this shape is too long or diagonal for one grid, so it is made in chunks that are joined into one level. Generate downloads every chunk first; the previews show a coarser overview.
tiles.bigDesktop: Big: this shape covers {km2} km², more than the website allows ({maxKm2} km²). The desktop app builds it, but it may take a long time and need a lot of disk space.
tiles.anchorCenterTitle: Anchor on the centre of all tiles
tiles.anchorHint: The anchor is the point that sits on the location above. Click a tile or Centre to move it: the tiles stay where they are.
